title: Vectors (1): Scalars, Notation and Operations
summary: The difference between scalars and vectors, the ways of writing a vector, and adding, subtracting and scaling vectors with components.

p: A scalar has magnitude (size) only. A vector has magnitude and direction. Scalars: distance (5 km), time (30 s), mass (10 kg), speed (60 km/h). Vectors: displacement (5 km north), force (10 N east), velocity (80 km/h west). A vector is drawn as a line with an arrowhead: the length shows the magnitude and the arrow shows the direction.
Geometric form: AB (an arrow over the letters) is the vector from A to B. We also write a single bold or underlined letter, such as a.
Column form: the vector from the origin to the point (x, y) is written as a column with x on top and y below.
Unit vector form: a = xi + yj, where i = (1, 0) is the unit vector along the x-axis and j = (0, 1) is the unit vector along the y-axis. So 3i − 4j is the same as the column (3, −4).
The zero vector 0 = (0, 0) has no size and no direction. The negative vector −a has the same magnitude as a but the opposite direction. If a = (x, y) then −a = (−x, −y).

Add or subtract the components: (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c, b + d) and (a, b) − (c, d) = (a − c, b − d). Graphically, the triangle law: place p and q head to tail; the resultant p + q goes from the start of p to the end of q.
For a scalar k and a = (x, y): ka = (kx, ky). If k > 1 the vector stretches. If 0 < k < 1 it shrinks. If k < 0 the direction reverses.
Example 3. Given p = 2i + 3j and q = 4i − 5j, find r such that 2p + r = 3q. r = 3q − 2p = (12, −15) − (4, 6) = (8, −21) = 8i − 21j.

title: Vectors (2): Magnitude, Direction and Unit Vectors
summary: How to find the magnitude and direction angle of a vector (with quadrant care) and how to find a unit vector.

p: For a = (x, y), the magnitude (length) is |a| = √(x² + y²). It is just Pythagoras' theorem.
The direction angle θ (measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis) is found from tan α = |y/x|, where α is the acute reference angle. Then use the signs of x and y to choose the quadrant.
Quadrant I (+, +): θ = α. Quadrant II (−, +): θ = 180° − α. Quadrant III (−, −): θ = 180° + α. Quadrant IV (+, −): θ = 360° − α.
A unit vector has magnitude 1. The unit vector in the direction of a is â = a ÷ |a|. Example: a = 3i + 4j has |a| = 5, so â = (3/5)i + (4/5)j. Check: √(9/25 + 16/25) = 1.

Example 1. Find the magnitude and direction of v = (−5, 12). |v| = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13. tan α = 12/5 = 2.4, so α = 67.38°. x < 0 and y > 0, so the vector is in the second quadrant: θ = 180° − 67.38° = 112.62°.
Example 2. The unit vector in the direction of w = i − 2j. |w| = √(1 + 4) = √5. ŵ = (1/√5)i − (2/√5)j = (√5/5)i − (2√5/5)j.
Example 3. Magnitude of p = 5i + 12j: √(25 + 144) = 13.
Example 4. Unit vector of v = (3, 0): |v| = 3, so v̂ = (1, 0) = i.
Example 5. Magnitude and direction of a = (−1, −1). |a| = √2. α = 45°, third quadrant, θ = 180° + 45° = 225°.
Example 6. Unit vector of b = 4i − 3j: |b| = 5, b̂ = (4/5)i − (3/5)j.
Example 7. If v = (k, 8) and |v| = 10, find k. k² + 64 = 100, so k² = 36 and k = 6 or −6.
Example 8. The unit vector of p = (−3, 4): |p| = 5, p̂ = (−3/5, 4/5).

title: Vectors (3): Laws of Addition, Position Vectors and Resolution
summary: The triangle and parallelogram laws, position vectors and the vector between two points, and resolving a vector into components.

p: If two vectors are shown by two sides of a triangle taken in order, their resultant is the third side, taken in the opposite order. AB + BC = AC.
If two vectors a and b start from the same point, their resultant is the diagonal of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are a and b. The other diagonal is a − b or b − a, depending on direction.

img.alt: Two diagrams: the triangle law with vectors a and b placed head to tail and resultant a + b closing the triangle, and the parallelogram law with a and b from one point and the diagonal a + b
img.cap: The triangle law (left) and the parallelogram law (right).

p: The position vector of a point P(x, y) is OP = xi + yj, the vector from the origin. The vector from A to B is AB = OB − OA = (x₂ − x₁)i + (y₂ − y₁)j: 'head minus tail'. The position vector of the midpoint M of AB is OM = ½(OA + OB).

A vector v of magnitude |v| making an angle θ with the positive x-axis has components vₓ = |v| cos θ and vᵧ = |v| sin θ. So v = (|v| cos θ)i + (|v| sin θ)j. This is the basis of the analysis of forces and velocities in physics and engineering.

img.alt: A vector V at angle theta from the x-axis with a horizontal component V cos theta and a vertical component V sin theta forming a right triangle
img.cap: Resolving a vector into horizontal and vertical components.

p: Example 1. a = 2i + 5j and b = 6i − j are the position vectors of A and B. (a) AB = b − a = 4i − 6j. (b) The midpoint M: OM = ½(a + b) = ½(8i + 4j) = 4i + 2j.
Example 3. A force of 20 N acts at 30°. Fₓ = 20 cos 30° = 10√3 and Fᵧ = 20 sin 30° = 10, so F = 10√3 i + 10 j.
Example 4. A force has components 10 N east and 10√3 N north. |F| = √(100 + 300) = 20 N and tan θ = 10√3/10 = √3, so θ = 60°: 20 N at 60° north of east.
Example 6. In the parallelogram OABC with OA = a and OC = c: OB = a + c, and AC = c − a.

title: Vectors (4): The Scalar (Dot) Product
summary: How to multiply two vectors to get a number, the two forms of the dot product, and how to find the angle between vectors and test for perpendicular vectors.

p: The scalar (dot) product of two vectors is a number, not a vector. Component form: if a = a₁i + a₂j and b = b₁i + b₂j, then a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂. Geometric form: a · b = |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors.

Angle between vectors: equating the two forms gives cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Perpendicular test: if θ = 90°, cos θ = 0, so a · b = 0. If a · b = 0 (and neither vector is zero), the vectors are perpendicular.
Example 1. For a = 5i − 2j and b = 3i + 6j: a · b = 15 − 12 = 3.
Example 2. p = 3i + kj and q = 2i − 6j. For p ⊥ q: p · q = 6 − 6k = 0, so k = 1.
Example 3. Angle between a = 2i + j and b = 3i − j. a · b = 6 − 1 = 5. |a| = √5 and |b| = √10. cos θ = 5/(√5 × √10) = 5/√50 = 1/√2, so θ = 45°.
Example 4. u = (1, 1) and v = (1, −4). u · v = 1 − 4 = −3. |u| = √2 and |v| = √17. cos θ = −3/√34 = −0.5145, so θ = 121° (to the nearest degree).
Example 5. a = ti − 2j and b = (t + 3)i + 4j. For a ⊥ b: t(t + 3) − 8 = 0, so t² + 3t − 8 = 0 and t = (−3 ± √41)/2.
Example 6. If |a| = 4, |b| = 5 and the angle is 60°, a · b = 4 × 5 × cos 60° = 10.
Example 7. u = 2i − 8j and v = 4i + j: u · v = 8 − 8 = 0, so u ⊥ v.
Example 8. Given p = (−3, 4) and q = (5, k), find k if p ⊥ q: −15 + 4k = 0, so k = 15/4.
